name: The Hayes household — a reconstructed blacksmith (north division)
head: inf_blacksmith_north_02

arrival.note: NOT AN ARRIVAL, A BOUND. Nothing dates a hypothesised household, and a year would be a claim nobody made. `not_later_than` the scene date states the only thing the inference carries: the town's need is measured on 1 July 1835, so the household is posited as being here by then and at no stated time before it.

party_size_on_arrival.note: Not claimed. The layer infers households, not families: the person entries here are the ones the trade argument requires and nothing counts wives or children, because counting them would multiply a hypothesis by an invention.

origin.note: Not claimed. Where a hypothesised resident came from is unknowable by construction, and the documented layer's origins (Vermont, Washington, Ann Arbor) are evidence about those men and not a distribution to sample from.

reason_for_coming.note: Not claimed for the person. The reason the HOUSEHOLD is in the dataset is the trade argument in research_note, which is a statement about the town and not about a motive.

lives_at.note: THE HOUSEHOLD IS HOUSED, WHICH IS THE POINT OF THE LAYER. recon_1835_north_d6_021 is an anonymous reconstructed roof already standing on the plat, adopted rather than duplicated: its existence, position and footprint stay conjectural and the adoption adds only the occupant argument. Which roof of the right family and district a hypothesised household occupies is not evidence about that roof; the household needed a dwelling and the programme assigned it one.

works_at.note: recon_1835_north_w1_018 is an anonymous reconstructed roof already standing on the plat, adopted rather than duplicated: its existence, position and footprint stay conjectural and the adoption adds only the occupant argument. The workplace is assigned from the reconstruction schedule's workshop and store families for this trade.

present_on_scene_date.note: Presence on the scene date IS the hypothesis: this household exists in the dataset because the town of 1 July 1835 demonstrably needed households of this trade. It is not a finding about anybody's whereabouts.

persons.name: Martin Hayes

occupation.note: THE OWNER'S OWN EXAMPLE, AND THE ARITHMETIC IS ALREADY IN THE DOCUMENTED LAYER. Five smiths are documented - Asahel Pierce, David McKee at the agency, Matthias Mason of 'Mason & Co.', Lemuel Brown, and the Rev. Mr See whose tools Pierce bought - and the reconstruction schedule allows six W1 blacksmith shops. This parcel builds Mason's documented third smithy and infers three more smith households, which brings the town to the schedule's six shops exactly: the smithies the wagon, plough and horse traffic of a town of 3,265 requires beyond the ones the sources happen to name.

persons.note: HYPOTHESISED, AND NOT A PERSON. name_basis.note: THE NAME IS INVENTED. No source names this resident, and this field is not a finding about anybody — it is a label so that a reconstructed household reads as a household rather than as a row in a table. It was drawn from the Irish pool in data/reconstruction/1835_invented_name_pools.json, which is seeded from the names of the 76 ATTESTED residents this project holds — real people, named from cited sources — so that an invented resident is named the way this town's documented residents were actually named rather than the way a story would name one. The community was drawn WITHOUT a weighting that any source supports. The proportions of the documented layer, which is overwhelmingly New England and New York with an older French colonial presence and a small Irish one. Applied to every trade for which no source speaks to who did the work. The evidence for the pool itself: Present in the documented layer but thinly: one attested resident's origin is given as 'County Kerry, Ireland, by way of Lancashire, Dublin, Quebec, Montreal, New York, Virginia and Newark', and the attested surnames Egan and Casey belong to this stock. THE WEIGHTING TOWARD LABOURING TRADES IS ITSELF AN INFERENCE and is marked as such wherever it is applied: the Illinois and Michigan Canal contracts were not let until 1836, so the large Irish labouring population of the later 1830s is arriving around and after the scene date rather than established by it. What the pool claims is that Irish names belong in this town on 1 July 1835, which the documented layer supports; it does not claim any particular trade was Irish.

research_note: RECONSTRUCTED HOUSEHOLD - second of 3 blacksmith households in this layer, in the north division. THE OWNER'S OWN EXAMPLE, AND THE ARITHMETIC IS ALREADY IN THE DOCUMENTED LAYER. Five smiths are documented - Asahel Pierce, David McKee at the agency, Matthias Mason of 'Mason & Co.', Lemuel Brown, and the Rev. Mr See whose tools Pierce bought - and the reconstruction schedule allows six W1 blacksmith shops. This parcel builds Mason's documented third smithy and infers three more smith households, which brings the town to the schedule's six shops exactly: the smithies the wagon, plough and horse traffic of a town of 3,265 requires beyond the ones the sources happen to name. METHOD: the count comes from the occupation census in data/reconstruction/1835_inferred_household_programme.json, which calibrates every trade against three things this project already holds - the 1835 town census (3,265 people, 398 dwellings), Andreas's roster of the fall of 1833 (about fifty named people, most with a trade, in a settlement of some 350), and the reconstruction specification's roof schedule, whose workshop and store family targets are treated as the ceiling on a trade rather than as its measure. Every count is stated NET of the documented layer: this dataset infers a tradesman only where it cannot name one.
